questions.q: What is Hive-style partitioning in S3?
options: Encoding a partition column and its value directly into the key prefix, as column=value
A real nested directory structure S3 maintains under the hood
A special S3 storage class for partitioned data
A Glue-only feature that doesn't work with Athena
questions.explain: Hive-style partitioning is a naming convention (year=2024/month=01/...) in the key prefix that query engines like Athena and Glue recognize as partition columns.

options: A query engine skipping non-matching partitions instead of scanning them
Deleting old partitions automatically after 90 days
Compressing partition data to save storage cost
Merging small partitions into larger ones
questions.explain: Partition pruning means the query engine uses the partition structure to read only matching prefixes, skipping everything else — dramatically reducing data scanned.

questions.q: Why does partition pruning matter specifically for Athena's cost, not just its speed?
options: Athena bills per TB scanned, so an unpruned query directly costs more money, not just more time
Athena charges a flat monthly fee regardless of data scanned
Athena has no cost implications tied to partitioning
Athena only charges for compute time, never for data scanned
questions.explain: Athena's pricing model bills per TB of data scanned, so failing to prune partitions increases the dollar cost of every query, not just its latency.

questions.q: What's the practical downside of partitioning a table by year/month/day/hour when it only receives ~200 rows per day?
options: Catalog bloat and many tiny objects, where planning overhead can outweigh the pruning benefit
There is no downside — finer partitioning is always strictly better
Athena would refuse to query a table partitioned this finely
It would violate S3's maximum partition depth limit
questions.explain: Over-partitioning a low-volume table creates many small partitions and objects, bloating the Glue Catalog and adding query-planning overhead that can exceed any pruning gains.

questions.q: Where do partition columns from a Hive-style key prefix get registered as usable table metadata?
options: The Glue Data Catalog
Inside the Parquet file headers themselves
An S3 bucket policy
IAM role trust policies
questions.explain: Glue crawlers register the key-prefix partition columns (like year, month, day) into the Glue Data Catalog as table metadata, even though the values live only in the key, not the file contents.
